result: A trained tasting panel of 11 panellists conducted 3,973 sensory trials on 700 botanical drugs from De Materia Medica, using 22 chemosensory descriptors to assess taste and flavor qualities. The panel reported 10,463 individual perceptions, with bitter being the most frequently reported quality (39% of samples) and mucilaginous the least (3.2%). Most perceptions were weak intensity (50%), with 37% medium and 13% strong. The study also extracted 46 therapeutic uses across 25 categories from DMM, with a mean of 6.3 uses per drug.
evaluation: Claims C40-C64 describe the sensory panel methodology and descriptive statistics from the tasting trials. The methods are clearly documented with specific numbers of panellists, trials, and samples. The frequency distributions of chemosensory qualities and their intensities are quantitative results directly from the data collection. These methodological and descriptive claims are well-supported by the experimental design.

result: Using phylogenetic generalized linear mixed models with strong phylogenetic signal (h² > 0.9), the study found that chemosensory intensity positively predicts therapeutic versatility (px < 0.001), while chemosensory complexity negatively predicts therapeutic versatility (px = 0.026). These relationships hold while controlling for phylogenetic non-independence among plant species.
evaluation: Claims C65-C67 present the core statistical findings from the PGLMMs relating chemosensory properties to therapeutic versatility. The positive relationship with intensity and negative relationship with complexity are both statistically significant with reported p-values. The high phylogenetic signal (h² > 0.9) validates the need for phylogenetic correction. These results are supported by appropriate statistical methods and are visualized in Figure 2.

result: Specific chemosensory qualities show differential associations with therapeutic versatility. Bitter (px = 0.013), starchy (px = 0.017), musky (px = 0.013), sweet (px < 0.018), and soapy (px = 0.002) qualities were positively associated with versatility, while sourness was negatively associated (px < 0.001). Notably, the most versatile drugs were not exclusively bitter-tasting, contradicting common assumptions about medicine.
evaluation: Claims C68-C74 report statistically significant associations between individual chemosensory qualities and therapeutic versatility from the PGLMM analysis. All associations have reported p-values below 0.05. The finding that versatile drugs are not only bitter (C69) is an important inference supported by the data showing multiple non-bitter qualities also predict versatility. These results challenge conventional wisdom about medicinal taste.

result: Nearly all therapeutic uses (except 'gynaecology – other') are significantly associated with at least one chemosensory quality, with 99 positive associations and 50 negative associations identified across all therapeutic uses. These associations often show high magnitude of effect.
evaluation: Claims C75-C77 summarize the comprehensive results from 46 probit models testing associations between chemosensory qualities and individual therapeutic uses. The quantitative counts (99 positive, 50 negative associations) are directly from the statistical analysis shown in Figure 3. The near-universal finding of at least one significant association per therapeutic use demonstrates the pervasive predictive power of chemosensation.

result: Sour taste shows 12 negative associations with therapeutic uses, including significant negative associations with treatment of coughs (px = 0.038), other respiratory problems (px = 0.042), and pain management (px = 0.021). These patterns are consistent with known physiological effects of acids, including acid-triggered coughing in airways and nociception from acidic solutions on lesions.
evaluation: Claims C85-C93 present specific statistical associations for sour taste and provide mechanistic interpretations based on cited physiological knowledge. The statistical associations are supported by the PGLMM results. The mechanistic explanations (C88-C90, C93) are reasonable inferences connecting the statistical patterns to established physiology from cited sources (Kollarik et al., 2007; Irwin, 2006), though these remain interpretations rather than direct experimental tests.

result: Sweet and starchy drugs show high therapeutic versatility (13 and 12 positive associations respectively), influenced by the overlap between medicinal and food uses. The 96 drugs specifically mentioned for food show positive associations with starchy, nutty, and salty qualities, and negative associations with bitter, woody, and stinging qualities. Daily use of food items may have enabled more detailed understanding of their effects, leading to diversification of therapeutic uses.
evaluation: Claims C94-C102 present statistical associations for sweet and starchy qualities and their relationship to food use. The quantitative associations are supported by the PGLMM results. The inference that food use enabled better understanding of effects (C96, C98) is reasonable speculation based on the data patterns, though not directly tested. The statistical associations between food drugs and specific chemosensory qualities (C101-C102) are well-supported.

result: Sweet-tasting drugs are positively associated with pain treatment (px = 0.032), consistent with known analgesic effects of sweet sensations. Both starchy (px = 0.001) and salty (px = 0.002) drugs are associated with treating diarrhea and dysentery, paralleling modern oral rehydration therapy that uses glucose, starch, and electrolytes to exploit sodium/glucose co-transport mechanisms.
evaluation: Claims C103-C109 connect statistical associations to modern pharmacological understanding. The statistical associations (C104-C106) are supported by PGLMM results. The mechanistic explanations draw on cited modern medical knowledge (Kakeda et al., 2010; Thiagarajah et al., 2015; Binder et al., 2014) to interpret ancient practices. The parallel between ancient starchy/salty drug use for diarrhea and modern oral rehydration therapy is a compelling inference, though the ancient practitioners did not understand the molecular mechanisms.

result: Starchy drugs are positively associated with treating topical ulcers (px = 0.001), skin infections (px = 0.025), other skin conditions (px = 0.035), and animal bites (px = 0.001). Fresh Fabaceae seeds, often perceived as starchy, contain protease inhibitors that can inhibit bacterial proteases and control bacterial virulence during cutaneous infections.
evaluation: Claims C110-C115 present statistical associations for starchy drugs with dermatological uses and provide a mechanistic explanation. The statistical associations are supported by PGLMM results. The mechanistic explanation connecting Fabaceae protease inhibitors to antibacterial effects is supported by cited literature (Birk, 1996; Wink and Waterman, 2018; Frees et al., 2013; Culp and Wright, 2017), providing a plausible biochemical basis for the observed therapeutic patterns.

result: Bitter was the most frequently reported chemosensory quality, showing nine significant associations with therapeutic uses including a negative association with foods. Not all bitter plant metabolites are toxic (e.g., iridoids, flavonoids, glucosinolates). Poisons showed no association with bitter taste but positive associations with aromatic, sweet, and soapy qualities, possibly because poisons were chosen to be unobtrusive.
evaluation: Claims C116-C125 present findings about bitter taste and its relationship to therapeutic uses and toxicity. The frequency data (C116) and statistical associations (C117-C118) are supported by the results. The observation that not all bitter compounds are toxic (C119-C120) is well-established. The finding that poisons lack bitter associations (C122-C124) is surprising and supported by the data, though the explanation (C125) is speculative. The evolutionary interpretation (C121) is reasonable speculation but not directly tested.

result: Bitter taste shows a strong positive association with sciatica treatment (px < 0.001), explained by anti-inflammatory pharmacology of bitter compounds. Bitter drugs for sciatica derive from disparate plant lineages containing different anti-inflammatory compound classes including iridoids, sesquiterpene lactones, triterpene saponins, and coumarins.
evaluation: Claims C126-C131 connect the statistical association between bitter taste and sciatica treatment to anti-inflammatory mechanisms. The statistical association is strongly supported (px < 0.001). The mechanistic explanation is supported by cited literature on anti-inflammatory properties of specific compound classes (Viljoen et al., 2012; Coricello et al., 2020; Gepdiremen et al., 2006; Wang et al., 2014; Kirsch et al., 2016). The phylogenetic diversity of plants with these properties strengthens the inference that the bitter-sciatica association reflects convergent pharmacological properties.

result: Many associations between chemosensory qualities and therapeutic uses are grounded in physiological effects mediated by chemesthesis and taste receptor pharmacology. Extraoral taste receptors, ectopic olfactory receptors, and TRP channels form a chemosensory network involved in homeostasis and disease response. Bitter taste receptors in airways mediate bronchodilation and ciliary movement, consistent with positive associations between bitter drugs and treatment of breathing difficulties (px = 0.027) and respiratory problems (px = 0.004).
evaluation: Claims C132-C137 propose that observed associations reflect extraoral chemosensory receptor functions. The hypothesis (C132) is supported by extensive cited literature on extraoral receptors (C133-C135: Foster et al., 2014; An and Liggett, 2018; Shah et al., 2009; Deshpande et al., 2010). The statistical associations between bitter and respiratory treatments (C136-C137) align with known bitter receptor functions in airways, providing strong support for the mechanistic interpretation. This represents a key insight connecting ancient practices to modern receptor pharmacology.

result: Drugs with fresh and cooling qualities are significantly associated with pain treatment (px = 0.01) and breastfeeding-related pain (px = 0.037), likely through TRP channel interactions. The TRPM8 channel mediates cold stimuli and is activated by cooling essential oil constituents producing analgesic effects. Cooling compounds like menthol and eucalyptol also act as counterirritants for respiratory irritation, explaining the association with breathing difficulty treatment (px = 0.04).
evaluation: Claims C138-C143 connect cooling sensations to pain relief and respiratory benefits through TRP channel mechanisms. The statistical associations are supported by PGLMM results. The mechanistic explanations are well-supported by cited literature on TRPM8 function and cooling compound pharmacology (McKemy et al., 2002; Behrendt et al., 2004; Proudfoot et al., 2006; Willis et al., 2011). This provides a clear molecular basis for the observed therapeutic patterns.

result: Burning and hot drugs show strong positive associations with musculoskeletal problems (px = 0.004) and vascular problems (px = 0.042), potentially through TRP channel-mediated analgesic and vasorelaxant effects. TRPV channels are involved in urinary bladder function, and TRPV1-knockout mice show altered urination patterns, potentially explaining the use of hot drugs for urinary problems (px = 0.047).
evaluation: Claims C144-C150 connect burning/hot sensations to multiple therapeutic uses through TRPV channel mechanisms. The statistical associations are supported by PGLMM results. The mechanistic explanations are supported by cited literature on TRPV channel functions (Marwaha et al., 2016; Aroke et al., 2020; Montell, 2005; Pires and Earley, 2017; Birder et al., 2002). The inference connecting TRPV function to urinary problem treatment (C150) is reasonable but more speculative than the pain and vascular associations.

result: Bitter taste shows positive associations with humoral management (px = 0.004) and liver problems/jaundice (px = 0.002), explained by uses intended to purge bitter bile. These ancient uses correspond to modern choleretics and cholekinetics. However, some humoral management drugs have strong emetic and purgative effects reflecting toxicity, and were abandoned along with humoral therapy.
evaluation: Claims C152-C158 connect bitter taste to humoral medicine practices and their modern equivalents. The statistical associations are supported by PGLMM results. The interpretation connecting ancient bile-purging to modern choleretics (C154-C155) is a reasonable inference bridging historical and modern pharmacology. The acknowledgment that some humoral drugs were toxic and abandoned (C156-C158) provides important context about the limitations of ancient practices.

result: Astringent and woody qualities show positive associations with diarrhea/dysentery treatment (px = 0.029 and 0.019) and vaginal discharge (px < 0.001), consistent with fluid-controlling and drying effects. Conversely, astringency shows negative associations with conditions requiring fluid flux, including fever (px = 0.045), humoral management (px = 0.02), urinary problems (px < 0.001), and cough (px = 0.002).
evaluation: Claims C159-C168 present a coherent pattern of astringent drug uses aligned with their perceived drying properties. All statistical associations are supported by PGLMM results. The pattern of positive associations with conditions requiring fluid control and negative associations with conditions requiring fluid flux demonstrates internal consistency. The correlation between woody and astringent qualities (C161) is supported by citation (Scalbert et al., 1989). This represents a clear example of how sensory properties guided therapeutic logic.

result: Remedies for dropsy and edema (diuretics) are negatively associated with salty tastes (px = 0.023), consistent with the known effect of salt intake aggravating fluid retention and edema.
evaluation: Claims C169-C170 present a straightforward association between salty taste and diuretic use that aligns with basic physiological knowledge. The statistical association is supported by PGLMM results. The mechanistic explanation (C169) is well-established medical knowledge. This represents a clear example where ancient therapeutic logic aligns with modern understanding of salt and fluid balance.

result: Chemosensation is strongly predictive of therapeutic use in ancient botanical medicine. Drugs with high therapeutic versatility have simple yet intense tastes and flavors, and 21 of 22 chemosensory qualities predicted at least one therapeutic use. Ancient drug uses were based on observed physiological effects often consistent with modern understanding of chemesthesis and taste receptor pharmacology, despite fundamentally different disease theories.
evaluation: Claims C4-C7 and C9 represent the main conclusions of the study, synthesizing the statistical findings and mechanistic interpretations. These conclusions are well-supported by the comprehensive statistical analyses showing: (1) intensity-versatility relationship (C65), (2) complexity-versatility relationship (C66), (3) 21/22 qualities predicting uses (C6, C75), and (4) multiple specific associations consistent with modern receptor pharmacology (C132-C150). The inference that ancient uses reflected observed physiological effects (C9) is strongly supported by the convergence of statistical patterns with modern mechanistic understanding.

result: Chemosensory qualities and their physiological effects help explain the persistence of humoral medicine until the 19th century. The study demonstrates that chemosensory perception connects ancient therapeutic knowledge with modern science, offers a blueprint for macroscale re-evaluation of pre-scientific knowledge, and points toward a central role for taste and flavor in medicine, highlighting the potential of chemosensory pharmacology in herbal medicine development.
evaluation: Claims C171-C172 and C179-C182 present the broader implications and conclusions of the study. These are supported by the comprehensive demonstration that ancient therapeutic patterns align with modern understanding of chemosensory receptor pharmacology. The claim about explaining humoral medicine's persistence (C171) is a reasonable inference from the findings. The methodological contribution (C181) and potential for future applications (C172, C182) are appropriate conclusions from the successful application of phylogenetic methods to this question.

result: The study applied phylogenetic generalized linear mixed models (PGLMMs) to test relationships between chemosensory qualities and therapeutic uses while accounting for phylogenetic non-independence. All models showed high heritability values (h² > 0.9), demonstrating strong phylogenetic signal and the importance of accounting for species' shared ancestry.
evaluation: Claims C42, C67, C196-C197 describe the statistical methodology and its validation. The use of PGLMMs is appropriate for data with phylogenetic structure. The high heritability values (h² > 0.9) across all models validate the methodological choice and demonstrate that phylogenetic relationships strongly influence both chemosensory properties and therapeutic uses. This methodological rigor strengthens confidence in the results by properly accounting for statistical non-independence.

result: The study collected 700 botanical drugs (ca. 70% of those in DMM) from 407 species between 2014-2016, with vouchers deposited in herbaria. A trained panel of 11 volunteers assessed chemosensory qualities using Conventional Profiling with a 4-point ordinal scale, following ethical guidelines. Therapeutic uses were extracted from Matthioli's 1568 edition of De Materia Medica.
evaluation: Claims C183-C195 describe the data collection and experimental procedures. The methods are clearly documented with appropriate detail including sample sizes, training procedures, ethical approvals, and data sources. The 70% coverage of DMM drugs (C184) represents substantial sampling. The sensory analysis methodology follows established protocols (Conventional Profiling). Ethical approvals and informed consent (C189-C190) were obtained. These methodological details support the validity and reproducibility of the study.

result: The study acknowledges limitations including inability to address all associations and dependence on published pharmacological data for explanations. Drugs with chemosensory profiles not aligned with therapeutic uses might work beyond chemosensory pharmacology, and associations may overlap with non-chemosensory mechanisms. The approach demonstrates the power of phylogenetic methods applied to human behavior and plant property assessment.
evaluation: Claims C173-C178 acknowledge study limitations and methodological contributions. The limitations (C177) are appropriately recognized - not all associations can be explained and mechanistic interpretations rely on literature. The acknowledgment that some drugs may work through non-chemosensory mechanisms (C173-C174) shows appropriate scientific caution. The example of opium (C175-C176) illustrates this complexity. The claim about demonstrating phylogenetic methods' power (C178) is justified by the successful application to this interdisciplinary question.
